gap: No result ChatGPT got states that an ATX 3.1 desktop power supply only has to ride through 12 ms of lost AC at full load. Jackery rates the HomePower 1000 v2 and HomePower 1000 Plus v2 to switch over in under 10 ms, which is inside that window. The Explorer 1000 v2 (20 ms) and Explorer 2000 v2 (under 20 ms) are not.
standout_why: I compared five results. Notebookcheck's Explorer 1000 v2 article gives the 20 ms switchover and warns that some devices can't tolerate it, but it names no threshold. GearBrain's HomePower 1000 Plus V2 article gives ≤10 ms and makes no link to PCs or power supply hold-up. TechRadar's article was truncated in the fetch. ProToolReviews returned 403. The 10adventures, REI, jackery.com blog and Yahoo results I did not open, and they are not in the comparison. Of the pages compared, none ties the switchover time to the ATX hold-up requirement, and none says which Jackery models fall inside it.
decides: If the shopper wants the Jackery to sit between the wall and a desktop PC or NAS as a UPS, pick from the HomePower v2 line. The HomePower 1000 v2 ($549, under 10 ms) and HomePower 1000 Plus v2 ($669, under 10 ms, expandable to about 11 kWh) switch inside the 12 ms ATX 3.1 floor. The Explorer 1000 v2 (20 ms) and Explorer 2000 v2 (under 20 ms) take longer than even the older 17 ms ATX 3.0 full-load requirement, so a heavily loaded PC isn't guaranteed to stay on. Jackery's own Explorer 2000 v2 page says the computer and NAS 'stay online' anyway. For camping or a fridge, where a 20 ms gap doesn't matter, this mechanism doesn't change the pick.

findings.label: ATX 3.1 PSU hold-up time requirement
findings.value: 12 ms at full load (ATX 3.0: 17 ms at full load); ATX 3.1 recommends 17 ms at 80% load
findings.source_title: Seasonic: Differences Between ATX 3.0 and ATX 3.1 Standards
findings.note: Seasonic table row 'Voltage Power-Off Retention Time': ATX 3.0 '17ms at full load', ATX 3.1 '12ms at full load' with '17ms at 80% load recommended'. This is the minimum the spec guarantees at full load. A lighter load may ride through longer, but that isn't guaranteed.

findings.label: Why Intel set 12 ms
findings.value: Intel checked with UPS makers that their switch-to-battery time is under 12 ms
findings.source_title: Hardware Busters: ATX v3.1 & PCIe CEM 5.1 are official
findings.note: Article dated 2023-09-17. Quote: 'Intel contacted UPS manufacturers to confirm that the switch to battery time is lower than 12ms.' The author disagrees with the cut from 17 ms.
